questions.title: 50. What is React reconciliation?
questions.summary:
◦ Reconciliation = R^ determines what changed between previous and next UI.
◦ Uses element type + key to preserve or replace identity.
questions.answer:
◦ Reconciliation = R^ process of comparing new UI descriptions w1 existing Fibers.
◦ Determines which C^s and host nodes can be reused, updated, or replaced.
◦ Type + key determine whether children match in their parent context.
◦ Matching identity generally preserves C^ state.
◦ Changed identity can trigger remount + state reset.
◦ Reconciliation calculates changes; commit applies them.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ An update schedules work on the Fiber tree.
◦ R^ executes C^s to produce new elements.
◦ Child reconciliation matches new elements against existing child Fibers.
◦ Same type + matching key → reuse eligible Fiber + preserve state.
◦ Different type/key → replace Fiber + reset affected state.
◦ R^ tracks placement, update, and deletion work.
◦ Commit phase applies necessary DOM changes.
pitfalls: ◦ Reconciliation ≠ DOM mutation.
◦ Keys only need to be unique among siblings.
◦ Index keys can cause state mismatches after reordering.
◦ Random keys force remounts.
◦ Same type alone does not guarantee preservation across different positions.
followUps: ◦ What happens when element type changes?
questions.recall: ◦ New Elements + Existing Fibers → Diff(type/key) → Reuse/Replace → Commit.

questions.title: 51. What is the Virtual DOM?
questions.summary:
◦ Virtual DOM = conceptual JS representation of UI.
◦ R^ uses element descriptions + Fiber to coordinate DOM updates.
questions.answer:
◦ Virtual DOM = conceptual in-memory representation of the desired UI.
◦ JSX creates R^ element descriptions rather than actual DOM nodes.
◦ R^ reconciles new descriptions against existing work.
◦ Fiber tracks C^ state, identity, and scheduled work.
◦ Commit applies necessary changes to the real DOM.
◦ Avoids blindly replacing the entire DOM tree.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ JSX compiles into element-creation calls.
◦ Elements describe type, props, and children.
◦ R^ maintains a Fiber tree representing current UI work.
◦ On updates, R^ reconciles new elements w1 existing Fibers.
◦ Matching identity allows reuse; changed identity may require replacement.
◦ DOM mutations occur during commit.
◦ Virtual DOM does not guarantee superior perf_nc in every scenario.
questions.code:
const element =

Hello

; // R^ element description, not a real DOM node.
pitfalls: ◦ Virtual DOM ≠ real DOM.
◦ R^ elements ≠ Fiber nodes.
◦ Virtual DOM ≠ automatic performance guarantee.
◦ Re-r() does not necessarily mutate DOM.
followUps: ◦ Does every re-r() update the DOM?
questions.recall: ◦ JSX → Elements → Fiber/Reconciliation → Commit → Real DOM.

questions.title: 52. What is React Fiber?
questions.summary:
◦ Fiber = R^ reconciliation architecture built around units of work.
◦ Enables priority-aware + interruptible rendering.
questions.answer:
◦ Fiber = R^ internal architecture for reconciliation and scheduling.
◦ Each Fiber represents work associated w1 a C^, Fragment, or host element.
◦ Stores props, state, relationships, and pending work.
◦ Supports splitting rendering into units of work.
◦ Enables R^ to prioritize, interrupt, resume, or restart render work.
◦ Completed work is committed to the host environment.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ Fiber nodes connect through child, sibling, and return pointers.
◦ R^ maintains current + work-in-progress representations.
◦ alternate connects corresponding Fibers between those representations.
◦ Lanes encode update priorities and pending work.
◦ Scheduler helps coordinate when rendering work executes.
◦ Render phase may be interrupted or restarted.
◦ Commit phase applies completed mutations synchronously.
pitfalls: ◦ Fiber is an internal architecture, not a public API.
◦ Fiber ≠ Virtual DOM exactly.
◦ Concurrent rendering ≠ multithreaded JS.
◦ Interruptible render ≠ interruptible commit.
◦ useTransition does not make synchronous calculations non-blocking.
questions.recall: ◦ Fiber → Work Units → Lanes → Scheduling → Interruptible r() → Commit.

questions.title: 53. How are Hooks related to Fiber?
questions.summary:
◦ H^ state belongs to the C^ Fiber.
◦ Call order maps H^ calls to their stored state.
questions.answer:
◦ H^ allow functional C^s to access R^ state and lifecycle-related capabilities.
◦ R^ associates H^ state w1 the C^ Fiber.
◦ H^ calls are matched by their order during r().
◦ Each C^ instance has its own H^ state.
◦ RoH require consistent H^ call order.
◦ Call H^ at top^lvl of C^s or CH^s.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ A functional C^ Fiber stores its hook list through memoizedState.
◦ H^ records are linked in call order for stateful hooks.
◦ During r(), R^ walks these records in the same order.
◦ useState/useReducer maintain update queues associated w1 hook records.
◦ setState schedules an update on the owning Fiber.
◦ Conditional H^ calls can shift hook positions and break state association.
◦ Different mounted instances have separate Fiber-associated hook data.
pitfalls: ◦ Never call H^ inside conditions or loops.
◦ Never call H^ after an early return that changes call order.
◦ H^ belong to C^ instances, not globally shared F() definitions.
◦ Not every H^ stores state in exactly the same internal form.
followUps: ◦ How does R^ know which state belongs to which H^?
◦ Why must H^ call order remain stable?
◦ What happens when two Counter C^s mount?
questions.recall: ◦ C^ Fiber → H^ records → Call Order → State/Queue → Re-r().

questions.title: 54. What controls update prioritization?
questions.summary:
◦ R^ prioritizes updates through lanes + scheduling.
◦ Urgent interactions can take precedence over transition updates.
questions.answer:
◦ R^ update prioritization is primarily coordinated through lanes and its scheduling system.
◦ Lanes represent update priority categories and pending work.
◦ Urgent updates, such as typing, generally receive higher priority than transitions.
◦ useTransition marks eligible state updates as non-urgent.
◦ useDeferredValue allows a less urgent part of UI to lag behind a changing value.
◦ R^ can interrupt lower-priority rendering to handle urgent work.
questions.underTheHood:
◦ setState creates an update associated w1 a lane.
◦ R^ tracks pending lanes on the root.
◦ Scheduling selects work according to priority and other constraints.
◦ Higher-priority work may interrupt lower-priority rendering.
◦ Interrupted rendering may resume or restart depending on circumstances.
◦ Commit applies a completed tree synchronously.
◦ React's scheduler coordinates execution, while lanes encode rendering priorities.
pitfalls: ◦ useTransition ≠ async/await.
◦ Transition updates cannot control text inputs directly.
◦ Priority does not guarantee a fixed execution time.
◦ Concurrent rendering ≠ parallel threads.
◦ startTransition marks synchronous state updates; updates after await need another startTransition.
followUps: ◦ Can R^ interrupt the commit phase?
questions.recall:
◦ setState → Lane → Schedule → Priority → Render → Commit.
◦ Urgent > Transition.
◦ useTransition → Non-urgent updates.
